input.cautions:
Where the literature disagrees, and where it fits this system badly.

1. The central disagreement: does written structure matter at all? The benchmark literature (IFScale, ManyIFEval, lost-in-the-middle, instruction-hierarchy work) says instruction count, position and conflict all degrade compliance. The one large field study of real agent config files (McMillan, arXiv:2605.10039, 1,650 sessions) found *none* of file size, instruction position, file architecture or adjacent-file contradiction produced a detectable effect, with affirmative-null Bayes factors for size and conflict. These can be reconciled — the field study measured a single trivial annotation target, not many simultaneous obligations, and its size range topped out at 500 lines, far below this corpus's ~160,000 words — but a reviewer should not assert that shortening or reordering a file will improve adherence. The evidence for that is benchmark evidence, not field evidence. The best-supported field finding is the opposite in character: compliance decayed ~5.6% in odds per additional unit of work within a session, regardless of how the rules were written.

2. "Does more specification help?" has no single answer in the sources. Gloaguen et al. found context files gave no general improvement at >20% cost; the same work found instructions *were* followed while repository overviews were useless — so the effect is content-type-specific, not dose-specific. Cai et al. found the opposite sign in a different setting: targeted rule updates lifted compliance from 49% to 72%. The reconciliation the evidence supports: specification that closes a genuine information gap pays; specification that restates what is already derivable costs without paying. That is a claim about the *marginal* document, not a licence to prune indiscriminately — and no source establishes a turning point in words, so any word-count target a reviewer sets is an engineering convention, not a research finding.

3. External validity is the biggest weakness. Every quantitative source measures task completion on benchmarks — SWE-bench issues, multi-document QA, format-constrained generation — where success is verifiable and the horizon is one task. This corpus's outputs are governance artifacts whose "success" is contested, long-horizon and partly about human coordination. A definition can be excellent for a human reader and expensive for an agent, and the literature only prices the second. Rating a governance corpus purely on agent-facing efficiency will systematically undervalue rationale, provenance and audit trail, which are load-bearing for the human authority even when they cost agent tokens. Factors that count words or tokens should be read as "what does this cost the agent", not "what is this worth".

4. Benchmark selection bias toward checkable rules. IFEval and its successors are built from *verifiable* instructions because those are the ones that can be scored. The literature therefore has a lot to say about form rules and almost nothing measured about judgment-shaping guidance ("prefer modular design"). The absence of evidence that guidance-style principles help is not evidence they don't; a corpus that excludes them because they fail a testability bar is making a decision the research does not license either way. Similarly, the prohibition-framing factor rests mainly on practitioner analysis rather than a controlled study — it is the weakest-sourced factor in the set and should be weighted accordingly.

5. Prompt-optimisation results (GEPA, APE) show automated search beats human-written instructions on scored tasks. They do not show that a corpus of governance definitions should be machine-optimised: the objective function that makes optimisation work does not exist here. Their usable implication is narrower and more uncomfortable — author intuition about what wording works is a poor predictor, so the absence of any measurement loop is a real defect even if the fix is not automated optimisation.

6. Two model-specific hazards for this system in particular. First, the sources on multi-agent architectures (4×/15× token multipliers, MAST's inter-agent misalignment category) mostly study parallel research fan-out; Anthropic explicitly notes multi-agent underperforms "on tasks requiring shared context or heavy interdependencies, like most coding work". A shop whose roles all operate on one shared corpus is closer to the bad case than the good one, and the multi-agent literature's positive results should not be read as endorsement of role proliferation. Second, the single-human-authority structure means several factors here (checker independence, handoff completeness, measurement loops) cannot be satisfied by adding people; they have to be satisfied by tooling, fresh contexts, or accepting a weaker check honestly recorded as weak.

7. Finally, the recursion. These factors are themselves prose rules applied by judgment, and every critique they encode — judgment load, unverifiable criteria, no measured outcome — applies to them. They are a diagnostic instrument, not a standard to adopt into the corpus; adopting them as governed definitions would add mass of exactly the kind they are meant to detect.

factors.name: Loaded-context budget per activity
factors.question: How many tokens must an agent hold to perform one step, and how many of those tokens are always-on rather than fetched when needed?
factors.source: Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (Sept 2025), https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents — "find the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome"; Hong, Troynikov & Huber (Chroma), "Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance" (14 Jul 2025), https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot — 18 frontier models, all degrade monotonically with input length well before the window fills; Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev & Vechev, "Evaluating AGENTS.md" (arXiv:2602.11988, Feb/Jun 2026) — context files raised inference cost "by over 20% on average".
factors.measurement: Token-count the exact set an agent holds at step entry: always-on block (compiled principles, CLAUDE.md, role definition) + step prompt + referenced definitions actually read. Report three numbers per activity: always-on tokens, step-specific tokens, and tokens-loaded-per-delivered-artifact. Flag any activity whose always-on share exceeds ~30% of its load, or whose total load exceeds what the step's output could plausibly justify. In this corpus the countable proxy is words: `wc -w` per process definition (range 804–6,562; median ~2,100) plus the compiled principle block on every session.
factors.why: Degradation is a function of tokens present, not tokens relevant. A healthy system pays context only where it changes the output; a sick one pays a fixed tax on every step for material most steps never use, and the tax is invisible because nothing meters it. The always-on/just-in-time split is the single cheapest structural fix available.

factors.name: Obligation count reaching one step
factors.question: How many independently checkable obligations bind a single agent step at once?
factors.source: Jaroslawicz, Whiting, Shah & Maamari, "How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow At Once?" (IFScale, arXiv:2507.11538, Jul 2025) — accuracy degrades steadily with instruction count, with threshold/linear/exponential decay profiles by model, omission errors dominating early and modification errors later; Kimura et al., "When Instructions Multiply" (ManyIFEval, EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv:2509.21051) — prompt-level accuracy (all instructions satisfied) falls consistently as count rises and is predictable from count alone via a beta-binomial model.
factors.measurement: Count obligations, not sentences: every clause a checker could independently mark pass/fail that binds this step — principle-set bullets in the always-on block, writing rules from the guideline, typedef fields, fitness criteria, step prompt directives. Sum them per step. Then compute the compounding estimate: if a step carries N obligations and per-obligation compliance is p, all-pass ≈ p^N. Score: ≤10 healthy, 10–25 watch, >25 expect silent omissions. Record which obligations are inherited (always-on) versus local.
factors.why: This is the mechanism behind "the corpus is too verbose" and it is countable in a way word count is not. All-obligations-satisfied is multiplicative, so adding a rule lowers the odds every other rule is honoured. It also predicts the observed failure shape: rules are not disputed, they are quietly dropped — omission, not defiance — so a system can look compliant while its tail obligations are dead letters.

factors.name: Novel-information ratio
factors.question: What fraction of a document tells the agent something it could not derive from the task, the artifact in front of it, or its own priors?
factors.source: Gloaguen et al., "Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?" (arXiv:2602.11988) — "providing context files does not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average… while instructions in the context files are well followed by coding agents, repository overviews, although popular and recommended by model providers, are not helpful"; summarised with figures at DAIR.AI, https://academy.dair.ai/blog/agents-md-evaluation — human-written files +4%, auto-generated −0.5% to −2%; auto-generated files improved 2.7% once duplicated repo docs were removed. Developer-written files averaged 641 words / 9.7 sections.
factors.measurement: Classify each paragraph: (a) non-obvious local convention or constraint, (b) restatement of something defined elsewhere in the corpus, (c) restatement of general good practice the model already knows, (d) rationale/narrative addressed to humans. Report the a-share. Healthy corpora are a-heavy. Also count cross-document restatements of the same rule (single-source violations) — grep a rule's distinctive phrase and count hits.
factors.why: This is the sharpest empirical result in the literature for a definition corpus: the part that pays is the surprising, repo-specific instruction; the part that costs without paying is the overview, the recap, the restated principle. It refines the verbosity hypothesis — the problem is not length as such but the ratio, and a 6,000-word process definition that is 80% category (a) may be fine while a 900-word one that is 80% (b)+(c) is pure drag.

factors.name: Enforcement locus (tool versus prose)
factors.question: For each rule, what actually stops a violation — a schema, a tool, a failing test, or only a sentence the agent is asked to remember?
factors.source: Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024), https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents — "Poka-yoke your tools. Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes"; Anthropic, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents", https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents — a JSON feature-list file chosen because the model "is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files", plus mandatory end-to-end test rituals rather than trusting self-reported completion; OpenAI, "A practical guide to building agents" (Apr 2025), https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf — guardrails as layered defence, with deterministic rules-based checks alongside LLM-based ones; Zhou et al., IFEval (arXiv:2311.07911) — the benchmark is built entirely from *verifiable* instructions, i.e. the class of rule a program can check.
factors.measurement: Tabulate every normative statement in the corpus against its enforcement: (1) structurally impossible to violate, (2) blocked by a tool/schema/lint at write time, (3) detected by an automated check after the fact, (4) checked by a fresh-context agent against stated criteria, (5) prose only, self-attested. Report the distribution. Then a second column: for each rule at level 4–5, does a violation produce any signal at all? In this corpus, contrast the 106 MUST/MUST NOT statements in `basis/` against what `lint_basis.py` can actually detect.
factors.why: Prose is the weakest available enforcement and the most expensive per unit of compliance — it costs context on every step and binds only probabilistically. Rules about form, presence, naming, sequence and completeness are exactly the rules a linter enforces at zero context cost and 100% reliability; spending prompt tokens on them is a category error. The health signal is the shape of the distribution: a corpus where nearly everything sits at level 5 has written a wish list, not a control system.

factors.name: Constraint integrity (who can waive)
factors.question: Can the party a constraint binds relieve itself of that constraint without anyone else acting?
factors.source: Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" (MAST, arXiv:2503.13657; NeurIPS 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657 — 14 failure modes over 1,600+ annotated traces, with an entire category for task verification failures: premature termination and inadequate verification; Anthropic, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" — agents "tended to make code changes, and even do unit testing, but would fail to recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end", fixed by forbidding status changes until an external test ran; Cai, Li, Liang, Li & Shahin, "Rule Taxonomy and Evolution in AI IDEs" (arXiv:2606.12231, Jun 2026) — across 83 projects and 7,310 rules, baseline artifact compliance with stated rules was 49.14%.
factors.measurement: For each constraint, name the role that declares it satisfied and the role it binds; count the cases where they are the same. Count self-declared exemptions in the artifact record (in this corpus: "accepted gap", self-asserted fitness passes, maker-stamped approval status) over a fixed window, and express as waivers per 10 artifacts. Separately count constraints whose enforcement tool was bypassed by an equivalent raw command (sed/grep in place of the artifact tool) — greppable in session transcripts.
factors.why: A self-attested constraint is a measurement of intent, not of the artifact, and the literature's ~49% baseline compliance says intent is roughly a coin flip. Worse, self-waiver is invisible in aggregate: the corpus still reads as governed while its rules have quietly become optional. This is the factor that separates a system with real constraints from one with a vocabulary of constraint, and it is measurable without any judgment about the rule's content.

factors.name: Judgment load per rule
factors.question: How much interpretation must an agent perform before it knows whether a rule is satisfied?
factors.source: Zhou et al., IFEval (arXiv:2311.07911) — 25 instruction types chosen because compliance is programmatically verifiable; the field measures what it can verify; Wang et al./"Assessing the Impact of Requirement Ambiguity on LLM-based Function-Level Code Generation" (arXiv:2604.21505, 2026) — Orchid benchmark, 1,304 tasks / 5,216 requirements over lexical, syntactic, semantic and vagueness ambiguity; GPT-4-class models drop >30% under ambiguous specifications and "lack the capability to identify or resolve such ambiguity autonomously"; Laban, Hayashi, Zhou & Neville, "LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation" (arXiv:2505.06120, May 2025) — models "make assumptions about underspecified details" rather than asking.
factors.measurement: Per rule, count: (a) defined terms that must be looked up before the rule can be applied (chase the glossary links), (b) evaluative adjectives with no operational definition ("appropriate", "sufficient", "minimal", "high-signal", "traceable"), (c) clauses per sentence. A rule requiring ≥2 lookups plus ≥1 undefined evaluative term is judgment-heavy. Report the share of judgment-heavy rules per document, and separately measure dispersion: give the same artifact to three fresh-context checkers and count verdict disagreements per 10 criteria.
factors.why: Ambiguity does not produce refusal or a question; it produces a confident divergent interpretation, and different agents diverge differently. That is the causal chain behind the hypothesis that dense rules get interpreted inconsistently and then waived — the waiver is downstream of the divergence. The inter-checker disagreement count is the empirical version of "idea density" and is the one measurement here that directly tests whether a rule is doing any work.

factors.name: Output-contract concreteness
factors.question: Does each step state the shape of what it must produce, with an example, or only the qualities the output should have?
factors.source: Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" — organise prompts into distinct sections including an explicit "Output description"; Anthropic, "How we built our multi-agent research system" (Jun 2025), https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system — each subagent task needs "an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries"; without them subagents duplicated work and misread scope; "ClarifyCodeBench" (arXiv:2607.00711) and ConInstruct/PRIME (arXiv:2606.22470) — models "seldom recognize contradictions or request clarification".
factors.measurement: Per agent-run step, score 0–4: objective stated; output format/schema named; at least one worked example or exemplar artifact referenced; boundaries stated (what this step must not decide). Report the share of steps scoring 4 and the share scoring ≤2. Count exemplars in the corpus: how many artifact types have a real, reachable specimen versus only a typedef.
factors.why: An output contract is the cheapest instruction a model can follow, because compliance is checkable by the model itself as it writes. Quality adjectives are the most expensive, because they require the model to simulate a checker. A corpus rich in typedefs but poor in exemplars has optimised for the expensive form — and exemplars also transfer tacit standards that no amount of rule text conveys.

factors.name: Conflict surface and stated precedence
factors.question: How many pairs of rules can bind the same decision and disagree, and does anything tell the agent which wins?
factors.source: Geng et al., "Control Illusion: The Failure of Instruction Hierarchies in Large Language Models" (arXiv:2502.15851, Feb 2025) — no tested model showed consistent adherence to system-level directives when user instructions conflicted, across model sizes and providers; "ManyIH-Bench" / many-tier instruction hierarchy (arXiv:2604.09443) — 853 agentic tasks with up to 12 privilege levels; best models below 50% accuracy, degrading as tiers increase; IHEval (arXiv:2502.08745). Counter-evidence: McMillan, "Instruction Adherence in Coding Agent Configuration Files" (arXiv:2605.10039, May 2026) found contradictions in adjacent config files produced no detectable adherence effect (affirmative-null BF10 0.05–0.10).
factors.measurement: Build the conflict matrix: for each decision an agent makes, list every document that constrains it (principles block, role definition, process step, guideline, typedef, fitness set). Count decisions constrained by ≥3 documents. Then search for a precedence statement covering each such overlap ('on conflict the source wins' is one; does anything rank principles against process steps?). Report: overlapping-constraint decisions, and the share with no stated precedence.
factors.why: Layered governance multiplies the tiers an agent must reconcile, and reconciliation accuracy falls as tiers grow. The practical effect is not visible disobedience but arbitrary resolution — which looks like inconsistency and gets diagnosed as a discipline problem. Note the disagreement in the literature: benchmark studies find conflict resolution unreliable, while the one field study of real config files found conflicts had no measurable effect on a simple compliance target. Treat conflict count as a design smell with contested effect size, not as a proven defect.

factors.name: Within-session compliance decay
factors.question: How much work does one agent context produce, and does compliance hold across it?
factors.source: McMillan, "Instruction Adherence in Coding Agent Configuration Files: A Factorial Study of Four File-Structure Variables" (arXiv:2605.10039, May 2026) — 1,650 Claude Code sessions, 16,050 observations; none of file size, instruction position, file architecture or adjacent-file contradiction produced a detectable effect, but "each additional function the agent generates is associated with approximately 5.6% lower odds of compliance per step (OR = 0.944)"; Laban et al. (arXiv:2505.06120) — 39% average performance drop single-turn to multi-turn across six tasks, aptitude −15% but unreliability +112%: "when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover"; Wang et al., "The Long-Horizon Task Mirage?" (HORIZON, arXiv:2604.11978, Apr 2026) — horizon-dependent degradation across 3,100+ trajectories.
factors.measurement: Count deliverables produced per context/session and per conversation turn-count; measure compliance on the first deliverable versus the last within the same session. Count how many governed artifacts are produced in one long session versus in fresh contexts. Also count steps that re-read their rules at point of use versus relying on the session's opening load.
factors.why: This is the largest measured effect in the only field study of real agent config files, and it reframes the whole debate: what degraded compliance was not how the rules were written or where they sat, but how far into the session the work happened. A system that batches many artifacts into one long context is spending its compliance budget on position in the session — and the early work will look governed while the late work quietly is not. It also means fresh-context checks are worth more than better-worded rules.

factors.name: Handoff payload completeness
factors.question: When work passes between roles or sessions, does the receiver get a self-sufficient package, or must it reconstruct intent from history?
factors.source: Anthropic, "How we built our multi-agent research system" — vague delegation ("research the semiconductor shortage") caused duplicated and misaimed subagent work; the fix was objective + output format + tool/source guidance + boundaries; Cemri et al., MAST (arXiv:2503.13657) — the inter-agent misalignment category covers conversation reset, proceeding on wrong assumptions instead of clarifying, task derailment, withholding crucial information, ignoring other agents' input; Anthropic, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" — a progress file plus git history so a fresh context "can quickly understand the state of work".
factors.measurement: For each handoff in the system (role to role, session to session, lead to executing unit), score the payload against the four elements, and record the carrier: durable artifact, structured record, or conversation transcript/model memory. Report the share of handoffs whose carrier is a transcript or summary. Count assumptions the receiver must make that the payload does not settle — read three real handoffs and list them.
factors.why: Multi-agent failure concentrates at the seams, and the seam's cost is paid silently: the receiver assumes rather than asks. In a multi-role definition shop, nearly every step is a handoff, so the per-handoff loss compounds across the chain. A handoff carried by a durable artifact is also the only kind that survives context loss, which is the normal condition of agent work.

factors.name: Verification independence and reproducibility
factors.question: Could a fresh context, given only the artifact and the stated criteria, reproduce the recorded verdict?
factors.source: Cemri et al., MAST (arXiv:2503.13657) — verification failures (premature termination, incomplete/incorrect verification) form one of the three top-level failure categories; Anthropic, "Writing effective tools for AI agents" (Sept 2025), https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents — build evaluations "grounded in real world uses" rather than trusting inspection; Anthropic multi-agent post — LLM-as-judge with an explicit rubric scored 0.0–1.0 in a single call, plus human testing because "manual testing catches edge cases that evals miss"; Wang et al. HORIZON (arXiv:2604.11978) — trajectory-grounded LLM-as-judge validated against human annotation (κ=0.84).
factors.measurement: Sample recorded checks and re-run them in a fresh context against the same criteria; count verdict flips. Score each check on: fresh context (yes/no), criteria external to the artifact (yes/no), evidence cited per criterion (yes/no), maker ≠ checker (yes/no). Report the share of checks that are reproducible on all four, and the flip rate.
factors.why: A check that cannot be reproduced is a ritual: it consumes a step, produces an approval stamp, and provides no information. Flip rate is the one number that tells you whether your quality apparatus is measuring the artifact or the mood of the checker — and if flip rate is high, every downstream claim resting on those approvals is unsupported.

factors.name: Instruction altitude
factors.question: Does a step tell the agent the goal and how success is recognised, or enumerate the procedure to reach it?
factors.source: Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" — the failure modes are hardcoded if-else logic creating "fragility and increases maintenance complexity" at one extreme and vague guidance that "fails to give the LLM concrete signals for desired outputs" at the other; the target is "specific enough to guide behavior effectively, yet flexible enough to provide the model with strong heuristics"; Anthropic, "Building effective agents" — "Start with simple prompts, optimize them with comprehensive evaluation, and add multi-step agentic systems only when simpler solutions fall short"; Li et al., "When Thinking Fails: The Pitfalls of Reasoning for Instruction-Following in LLMs" (arXiv:2505.11423, NeurIPS 2025) — explicit CoT prompting *degrades* instruction-following on IFEval and ComplexBench across 15 models, because reasoning "diverts attention away from instruction-relevant tokens".
factors.measurement: Per step, classify each directive as goal/criterion, heuristic, or procedure. Compute the procedure share. Count decision branches the agent must evaluate (conditions, routes, exception clauses) per step. Count prescribed intermediate artifacts that no downstream step consumes. Flag steps where procedure share >50% and the procedure is not tool-enforced.
factors.why: Over-specified procedure is doubly costly: it burns the context budget that the actual task needs, and it displaces attention from the constraints that matter — the mechanism is measured, not merely asserted. It is also the form of instruction that ages worst, because every procedural clause encodes an assumption about a situation that will change. Goal-plus-criterion instructions generalise; procedures must be maintained.

factors.name: Prohibition framing
factors.question: What share of the rules say what not to do, and does each prohibition name the compliant alternative?
factors.source: Zhou et al., IFEval (arXiv:2311.07911) establishes that positively specified, verifiable instructions are the tractable class; the practitioner literature on negative constraints (e.g. https://eval.16x.engineer/blog/the-pink-elephant-negative-instructions-llms-effectiveness-analysis) argues a prohibition must hold at every generation step while a positive format constraint must be satisfied once, and that a prohibition names an unbounded set — excluding a region of output space while specifying nothing about where to land. Note this specific claim rests on weaker evidence than the other factors here.
factors.measurement: Count MUST NOT / never / no X statements against MUST / positive directives (in this corpus: 21 MUST NOT and 5 SHOULD against 85 MUST and 13 MAY in `basis/`). For each prohibition, check whether an adjacent clause states the positive alternative. Report the prohibition share and the share of prohibitions with a stated alternative.
factors.why: A prohibition without an alternative leaves the model to pick a replacement by likelihood, which is precisely the default behaviour the prohibition was meant to override. Rewriting prohibitions as positive contracts usually also makes them checkable, which moves them up the enforcement ladder — so this factor is a cheap lever on two others.

factors.name: Evidence that the definitions work
factors.question: For any instruction in this corpus, is there a recorded before/after outcome showing it changed agent behaviour for the better?
factors.source: Anthropic, "Writing effective tools for AI agents" — evaluation tasks grounded in real use, then "collaborate with an agent to help analyze your results"; Anthropic multi-agent post — start with ~20 representative queries rather than waiting for a full dataset; Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov & Suhr, "Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design" (ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.11324) — semantically equivalent formatting variants swing accuracy by up to 76 points, so untested wording is an untested intervention; Agrawal et al., "GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning" (arXiv:2507.19457, 2025) and Zhou et al., APE (arXiv:2211.01910) — optimised instructions beat human-written ones on the large majority of tasks, i.e. author intuition about what wording works is a poor predictor; Gloaguen et al. (arXiv:2602.11988) conclude "any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment".
factors.measurement: Count instructions/definitions with any recorded outcome measure attached (an A/B, a before/after defect count, a compliance rate). Express as a percentage of the corpus. Record time since each definition's last outcome measurement, and the number of definition revisions made with no outcome evidence. Count the eval fixtures that exist at all — representative tasks the corpus can be run against.
factors.why: This is the factor that decides whether the corpus is an engineering artifact or a belief system. Author intuition about instruction wording is measurably unreliable, and formatting-level changes no author would consider meaningful can dominate outcomes — so a corpus grown entirely by reasoned revision, with no measured feedback, has no mechanism that distinguishes improvement from churn. It is also the factor most likely to explain a system that produces definitions faster than it produces working software.

factors.name: Corpus-to-output ratio
factors.question: How much definition mass exists per unit of delivered work, and is the ratio moving toward or away from delivery?
factors.source: Anthropic multi-agent post — "agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats", so architecture choices must be justified by task value; Gloaguen et al. (arXiv:2602.11988) — >20% cost overhead from context files regardless of quality, with no general success-rate gain; DAIR.AI summary — agents spend "14-22% more reasoning tokens and take 2-4 additional steps" when context files are present; Anthropic, "Building effective agents" — add machinery "only when simpler solutions fall short".
factors.measurement: Plot, over the system's life: cumulative words of governing definition versus count of delivered end-user artifacts (in this corpus: ~160,000 words in `basis/` over 26 days against zero shipped software). Track the derivative — definition words added per week against delivered outputs per week. Also compute definition mass per process actually executed, and count processes defined but never run.
factors.why: Governance mass has a real, measured cost per step and no guaranteed return, so its ratio to delivered output is the system-level fitness test that all the per-document factors roll up into. A ratio that grows without bound is the signature of a system whose feedback loop closes inside the definition layer — where writing definitions is checked by definitions about writing definitions — and which therefore has no error signal from the world. Processes defined but never run are pure carrying cost and the easiest place to cut.

Prompt reliability and optimisation:
- Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr, "Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design" (FormatSpread), ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.11324 — up to 76-point accuracy spread across semantically equivalent formats.
- Agrawal et al., "GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning", arXiv:2507.19457, 2025; Zhou et al., APE, arXiv:2211.01910 — optimised instructions beat human-written ones on most tasks.
data.cautions:
Where the literature disagrees, and where it fits this system badly.

1. The central disagreement: does written structure matter at all? The benchmark literature (IFScale, ManyIFEval, lost-in-the-middle, instruction-hierarchy work) says instruction count, position and conflict all degrade compliance. The one large field study of real agent config files (McMillan, arXiv:2605.10039, 1,650 sessions) found *none* of file size, instruction position, file architecture or adjacent-file contradiction produced a detectable effect, with affirmative-null Bayes factors for size and conflict. These can be reconciled — the field study measured a single trivial annotation target, not many simultaneous obligations, and its size range topped out at 500 lines, far below this corpus's ~160,000 words — but a reviewer should not assert that shortening or reordering a file will improve adherence. The evidence for that is benchmark evidence, not field evidence. The best-supported field finding is the opposite in character: compliance decayed ~5.6% in odds per additional unit of work within a session, regardless of how the rules were written.

2. "Does more specification help?" has no single answer in the sources. Gloaguen et al. found context files gave no general improvement at >20% cost; the same work found instructions *were* followed while repository overviews were useless — so the effect is content-type-specific, not dose-specific. Cai et al. found the opposite sign in a different setting: targeted rule updates lifted compliance from 49% to 72%. The reconciliation the evidence supports: specification that closes a genuine information gap pays; specification that restates what is already derivable costs without paying. That is a claim about the *marginal* document, not a licence to prune indiscriminately — and no source establishes a turning point in words, so any word-count target a reviewer sets is an engineering convention, not a research finding.

3. External validity is the biggest weakness. Every quantitative source measures task completion on benchmarks — SWE-bench issues, multi-document QA, format-constrained generation — where success is verifiable and the horizon is one task. This corpus's outputs are governance artifacts whose "success" is contested, long-horizon and partly about human coordination. A definition can be excellent for a human reader and expensive for an agent, and the literature only prices the second. Rating a governance corpus purely on agent-facing efficiency will systematically undervalue rationale, provenance and audit trail, which are load-bearing for the human authority even when they cost agent tokens. Factors that count words or tokens should be read as "what does this cost the agent", not "what is this worth".

4. Benchmark selection bias toward checkable rules. IFEval and its successors are built from *verifiable* instructions because those are the ones that can be scored. The literature therefore has a lot to say about form rules and almost nothing measured about judgment-shaping guidance ("prefer modular design"). The absence of evidence that guidance-style principles help is not evidence they don't; a corpus that excludes them because they fail a testability bar is making a decision the research does not license either way. Similarly, the prohibition-framing factor rests mainly on practitioner analysis rather than a controlled study — it is the weakest-sourced factor in the set and should be weighted accordingly.

5. Prompt-optimisation results (GEPA, APE) show automated search beats human-written instructions on scored tasks. They do not show that a corpus of governance definitions should be machine-optimised: the objective function that makes optimisation work does not exist here. Their usable implication is narrower and more uncomfortable — author intuition about what wording works is a poor predictor, so the absence of any measurement loop is a real defect even if the fix is not automated optimisation.

6. Two model-specific hazards for this system in particular. First, the sources on multi-agent architectures (4×/15× token multipliers, MAST's inter-agent misalignment category) mostly study parallel research fan-out; Anthropic explicitly notes multi-agent underperforms "on tasks requiring shared context or heavy interdependencies, like most coding work". A shop whose roles all operate on one shared corpus is closer to the bad case than the good one, and the multi-agent literature's positive results should not be read as endorsement of role proliferation. Second, the single-human-authority structure means several factors here (checker independence, handoff completeness, measurement loops) cannot be satisfied by adding people; they have to be satisfied by tooling, fresh contexts, or accepting a weaker check honestly recorded as weak.

7. Finally, the recursion. These factors are themselves prose rules applied by judgment, and every critique they encode — judgment load, unverifiable criteria, no measured outcome — applies to them. They are a diagnostic instrument, not a standard to adopt into the corpus; adopting them as governed definitions would add mass of exactly the kind they are meant to detect.
